The request

Subject: Two decisions under uncertainty: I need numbers I can defend
CF
Chief Financial Officer
To: Senior Business Risk Analyst (you)
Cc: Executive Risk Committee
Reply by Tue, Sep 29 · 11:59 PM ET

Hi Risk Analytics team,

We have two decisions in front of the Risk Committee: whether to adopt an automatic screening rule for customer churn, and how to invest in capacity. Our current plans lean on averages and gut feel. I want each answer tied to evidence, with units and denominators, and a plain statement of what the evidence can't tell us.

Specifically, I need answers to 5 questions:

  1. 1. Should we screen high-ticket accounts?
    Customer Success wants to flag accounts with heavy support-ticket volume for high-touch support. Using last year's 1,000 accounts, what is our baseline churn rate, and how much higher is it among high-ticket accounts? Someone told me "80%." Please check the denominator. And tell me plainly whether this shows screening would prevent churn.
    Part A
  2. 2. Large Hub or Modular Hub?
    Demand next year could be high, medium or low, and each hub pays off differently in each case. Which one has the higher expected value, by how much, and what would make us choose the other?
    Part B
  3. 3. Is our profit plan too optimistic?
    The plan assumes average demand. Simulate 1,000 demand scenarios. Does profit at average demand overstate what we should expect? How bad is a bad year (the 5th percentile)?
    Part C
  4. 4. How will you measure downside?
    The Committee cares about how often we lose money, not only the average. Show me the measure you'll use.
    Checkpoint
  5. 5. Option A or Option B for the next three years?
    A costs $1.0M up front; B costs $0.9M and is steadier. Using an 8% discount rate, compare expected NPV and the chance of losing money, recommend one, and tell me what would reverse your recommendation.
    Take-home

Please send me:

  • your completed workbook, and
  • a one-page memo that leads with the recommendation, cites every number with its unit and denominator, and discloses any AI use.

The account data and simulation inputs are attached. Thanks. I'm counting on this for the Committee.

Best,
Chief Financial Officer
CloudFlow Analytics

sheet IN-CLASS_Lab Part A · answers email question 1

Part A · Do high-ticket accounts churn more?

⏱ 8 min
From slide 24 → work this card → Back to slide 25 · bring: The exact conditional churn risk percentage of 35.3 percent for high-ticket accounts.

What the session covered · Section 1 Probability Rules and Conditional Business Risk

A contingency table sorts every account by two categories at once. The inside cells are joint counts; the row and column totals are marginal counts. From one table you can read four kinds of probability:

  • Marginal: one event across everyone. P(A)=row or column totalN P(A) = \dfrac{\text{row or column total}}{N}
  • Joint: both events together, across everyone. P(A∩B)=cell countN P(A \cap B) = \dfrac{\text{cell count}}{N}
  • Union: either event (or both). Subtract the overlap so it isn't counted twice. P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B) P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)
  • Conditional: one event within a group. The group's total becomes the denominator. P(A∣B)=P(A∩B)P(B) P(A \mid B) = \dfrac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}

Bayesian updating is the same idea, used to revise a baseline risk (the prior) after you see a signal. Base-rate neglect is the classic error: because most accounts renew, even a signal that catches 80% of churners flags more renewers than churners. So P(H∣C) P(H \mid C) and P(C∣H) P(C \mid H) are very different numbers.

⚠️ Most common mistake: reporting 80% as the churn risk. That is P(H∣C) P(H \mid C) in B17, the share of churners who had high tickets. The CFO asked for P(C∣H) P(C \mid H) : of the 272 high-ticket accounts, how many churned?P(C∣H)=96272=0.353≠P(H∣C)=96120=0.800 P(C \mid H) = \frac{96}{272} = 0.353 \quad\neq\quad P(H \mid C) = \frac{96}{120} = 0.800
Stuck? Three quick fixes
  • #NAME? The data table must be named Cohort with headers AccountID, Churn, HighTickets. Don't rename them.
  • Shows 3,529%. You multiplied by 100. Remove the *100; the cell is already a percentage.
  • Four counts don't add up to D11. Blank cells are missing, not "No". Keep the criteria exactly Yes and No.
Why does 80% shrink to 35.3%? (Bayes' rule worked through)P(C∣H)=0.80⏞P(H∣C)×0.12⏞P(C)0.80×0.12⏟churners flagged  +  0.20×0.88⏟renewers flagged=0.0960.272=0.353 P(C \mid H) = \frac{\overbrace{0.80}^{P(H\mid C)} \times \overbrace{0.12}^{P(C)}}{\underbrace{0.80 \times 0.12}_{\text{churners flagged}} \;+\; \underbrace{0.20 \times 0.88}_{\text{renewers flagged}}} = \frac{0.096}{0.272} = 0.353

The signal flags 96 churners but also 176 renewers, because renewers are 88% of the base. High-ticket accounts churn at about three times the 12.0% baseline. That supports screening them first. It does not show that screening would reduce churn.

sheet IN-CLASS_Lab Part B · answers email question 2

Part B · Large Hub or Modular Hub?

⏱ 10 min
From slide 42 → work this card → Back to slide 43 · bring: The optimal strategy selection and its expected value premium over the alternative.

What the session covered · Section 2 Expected Monetary Value and Decision Analysis

A decision separates what you control (the alternatives: Large Hub, Modular Hub) from what you don't (the states of nature: high, medium, low demand). States must be mutually exclusive and cover every possibility, so their probabilities sum to 1.

  • Payoff table: rows are alternatives, columns are states, and each cell is the net payoff v(dj,si) v(d_j, s_i) after capital costs.
  • Expected Monetary Value: the probability-weighted average payoff of one alternative. In Excel this is SUMPRODUCT(probabilities, payoffs).
  • Decision tree rollback: work right to left. At each chance node (circle), compute the EMV; at the decision node (square), keep the branch with the larger EMV and prune the other.
  • EMV is not an outcome: it's a long-run average; you will actually get one of the three payoffs. A committee that can't absorb the worst state may reject the higher-EMV branch.
  • Sensitivity: find the probability at which the preferred alternative flips (the tipping point).

Follow along: in SPSS, run the H2 block and leave H2 Capacity EMV Audit open.

SPSS block for this part · already in your syntax file

You do not type this: it is already in LAB02_SPSS.sps, the one syntax file you use all session. Once per SPSS session, run the CD line and the H0 block first (setup code in Part A). Then press Ctrl+F, search TITLE 'H2, select from the first comment line down to the last period, and choose Run › Selection. Green lines start with *: they are comments that explain the command below them, and SPSS ignores them. Every command ends with a period.

* Lecture connection: Expected Monetary Value .
* Why: Audit the probability weights and capacity EMVs using the same stated CloudFlow assumptions .
* How: Three retained cohort rows provide a reproducible workspace .
* How: Weighted payoffs are summed by capacity alternative .
* Read the result: Read the probability total, both EMVs and rolled-back node value in million dollars .
* Watch out: Do not mistake the largest state payoff for the largest EMV .
* Run: Select the complete H2 block .
* Run: Choose Run > Selection .
* Run: Locate H2 Capacity EMV Audit and read its listed values .
TITLE 'H2 Capacity EMV Audit'.
* Make a working copy so the original data stay untouched.
DATASET COPY CapacityAudit.
* Switch to the named dataset; the next commands work on it.
DATASET ACTIVATE CapacityAudit.
* Keep only the rows that meet the condition (others are deleted).
SELECT IF ($CASENUM <= 3).
* Declare new text variables.
STRING DemandState (A6).
* Start a block of commands that run only when the condition is true.
DO IF ($CASENUM = 1).
  COMPUTE DemandState='High'.
  COMPUTE StateProbability=.30.
  COMPUTE LargePayoff=12.
  COMPUTE ModularPayoff=9.
* Alternative condition inside a DO IF block.
ELSE IF ($CASENUM = 2).
  COMPUTE DemandState='Medium'.
  COMPUTE StateProbability=.50.
  COMPUTE LargePayoff=3.
  COMPUTE ModularPayoff=5.
ELSE.
  COMPUTE DemandState='Low'.
  COMPUTE StateProbability=.20.
  COMPUTE LargePayoff=-9.
  COMPUTE ModularPayoff=1.
* Close the DO IF block.
END IF.
* Create or overwrite a variable with a formula, row by row.
COMPUTE LargeWeighted=StateProbability*LargePayoff.
* Create or overwrite a variable with a formula, row by row.
COMPUTE ModularWeighted=StateProbability*ModularPayoff.
* Collapse rows into group summaries (one row per group).
AGGREGATE
  /OUTFILE=* MODE=ADDVARIABLES
  /ProbabilityTotal=SUM(StateProbability)
  /LargeHubEMV=SUM(LargeWeighted)
  /ModularHubEMV=SUM(ModularWeighted).
* Create or overwrite a variable with a formula, row by row.
COMPUTE RolledBackValue=MAX(LargeHubEMV,ModularHubEMV).
* Set how values display (width and decimals); the stored values do not change.
FORMATS StateProbability ProbabilityTotal (F5.3)
  LargePayoff ModularPayoff LargeHubEMV ModularHubEMV RolledBackValue (F8.2).
* Make the next transformation apply to the next procedure only.
TEMPORARY.
* Keep only the rows that meet the condition (others are deleted).
SELECT IF ($CASENUM=1).
* Print the listed variables row by row.
LIST VARIABLES=ProbabilityTotal LargeHubEMV ModularHubEMV RolledBackValue.
* Close a dataset you no longer need.
DATASET CLOSE CapacityAudit.
* Switch to the named dataset; the next commands work on it.
DATASET ACTIVATE CohortData.

⚠️ Most common mistake: picking the Large Hub because it has the biggest single payoff ($12M). The EMV rule weighs every state by its probability, and the Large Hub's -$9M low-demand state pulls its EMV down.EMV(Large)=0.30(12)+0.50(3)+0.20(−9)=3.30  <  EMV(Modular)=0.30(9)+0.50(5)+0.20(1)=5.40 \text{EMV}(\text{Large}) = 0.30(12) + 0.50(3) + 0.20(-9) = 3.30 \;<\; \text{EMV}(\text{Modular}) = 0.30(9) + 0.50(5) + 0.20(1) = 5.40
Stuck? Three quick fixes
  • EMV looks wrong. Payoffs must follow the same High, Medium, Low order as the probabilities in B7:D7.
  • Probabilities show 3000%. Type 30% or 0.3, not 30.
  • SUMPRODUCT shifts when you copy it. Keep the $ signs on $B$7:$D$7 so the probabilities stay fixed.
Why might the Committee still reject the higher-EMV hub? (optional)

EMV is a long-run average. CloudFlow builds one hub and gets one outcome. If a branch's worst state would breach a liquidity or covenant limit, a risk-averse committee can rationally reject it even when its EMV is higher. Here the Modular Hub also has the safer worst case ($1M vs. -$9M), so both views agree.

sheet IN-CLASS_Lab Part C · answers email question 3

Part C · Is profit at average demand too optimistic?

⏱ 12 min
From slide 65 → work this card → Back to slide 66 · bring: The simulated valuation gap between naive base-case profit and mean stochastic profit.

What the session covered · Section 3 Monte Carlo Simulation and the Flaw of Averages

The flaw of averages: plugging average demand into a nonlinear model does not give average profit. The capacity cap and salvage rule make profit nonlinear:

  • Upside is capped: when demand exceeds capacity, extra customers add nothing: sales =min⁡(D,Q) = \min(D, Q) .
  • Downside is not: when demand falls short, surplus units sell only at salvage: surplus =max⁡(Q−D,0) = \max(Q - D, 0) . So expected profit falls below profit at mean demand.
  • Monte Carlo simulation: runs the model many times with sampled demand. Inverse transform sampling turns a probability u u between 0 and 1 into a demand value: NORM.INV(u, mean, sd).
  • Summaries: mean profit, sample standard deviation, and the 5th-percentile profit, which is a dollar amount, not a percentage.
  • More trials don't fix a wrong model: they make the estimate more precise, not the assumptions more correct.

sheet IN-CLASS_Lab Part C · answers email question 4

Checkpoint · How will you measure downside?

⏱ 3 min
From slide 76 → work this card → Back to slide 80 · bring: State how the evidence supports this outcome: Evaluate operational capital investment trade-offs under stochastic demand, audit simulation models, and synthesize executive findings..

What the session covered · Section 4 Applied Risk Analysis and Simulation Modeling Workshop

Downside risk asks two things: how often outcomes fall below a benchmark (here, break-even) and how badly.

  • Loss probability: the share of simulated outcomes below zero. The denominator is every numeric outcome.
  • 5th percentile: how bad a bad year is, in dollars.
  • Standard deviation: measures spread in both directions, good and bad. Loss probability looks only at the bad side.
  • Decision rule from the session: if capital preservation governs, prefer the option with the lower loss probability and a safer 5th percentile, as long as expected value stays positive. If the firm can absorb losses, prefer the higher expected value.

sheet POST-CLASS_Part 1 · answers email question 5

Take-home · Option A or Option B for three years?

⏱ 45 min
At home → work this card → Submit

What the session covered · Section 4 Applied Risk Analysis and Simulation Modeling Workshop

The take-home reuses the Part C method on a three-year capital decision, using the three-layer model from the session: assumptions, then a one-trial engine, then 1,000 trials.

  • NPV: discount each year's cash flow at 8%. The initial investment happens at time zero, so it is subtracted outside Excel's NPV().
  • One shared shock per trial: the same zk z_k drives both options and all three years. That makes a fair side-by-side comparison, but it assumes a persistent business condition rather than independent years. Name that limitation in the memo.
  • Compare four numbers per option: expected NPV, standard deviation, 5th-percentile NPV and loss probability. The higher expected NPV is not automatically the answer; it depends on the Committee's risk tolerance.
  • Reversal condition: say what would reverse your recommendation, for example a different discount rate or risk tolerance.

⚠️ Most common mistake: putting the investment inside NPV(): Excel would discount it as if it were paid in year 1. Also: calling B23 a "percent change" (a gap between two probabilities is in percentage points), and dividing by 1000 instead of COUNT().
Stuck? Three quick fixes
  • All NPV rows are identical. D38 must use plain B2 (moves down), and E38/F38 must use $D38 (column locked, row free).
  • Loss probability is 0% or 100%. Check the sign: the formula starts with =-$B$10+NPV(.
  • Where's the finish check? Press Ctrl+G, type A1040. The Check your work box confirms structure, not your answer.

Python Parts A, B, C

Rebuilds the two-way table and all six probabilities, both EMVs and the 1,000-trial profit summary. Your printed numbers should match your workbook exactly (35.3%, 5.40, and the Part C summaries).

# LAB02 Parts A-C in Python (optional, not graded).
# Put this file next to cloudflow_churn_cohort.csv and reference_trials.csv.
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from statistics import NormalDist

# ---- Part A: two-way table and conditional churn risk ----
df = pd.read_csv("cloudflow_churn_cohort.csv", dtype=str, keep_default_na=False, na_values=[""])
pairs = df.dropna(subset=["Churn", "HighTickets"])          # complete pairs only; blanks are missing
print(pd.crosstab(pairs["HighTickets"], pairs["Churn"], margins=True, margins_name="Total"))

churn = pairs["Churn"].eq("Yes")
high = pairs["HighTickets"].eq("Yes")
p_c, p_h, p_both = churn.mean(), high.mean(), (churn & high).mean()
print(f"P(C)        = {p_c:.1%}")
print(f"P(H)        = {p_h:.1%}")
print(f"P(C and H)  = {p_both:.1%}")
print(f"P(C or H)   = {p_c + p_h - p_both:.1%}")
print(f"P(H | C)    = {(churn & high).sum() / churn.sum():.1%}   <- among churners")
print(f"P(C | H)    = {(churn & high).sum() / high.sum():.1%}   <- among high-ticket accounts")

# ---- Part B: payoff table and EMV ($ millions) ----
p = np.array([0.30, 0.50, 0.20])                           # high, medium, low demand
payoff = {"Large Hub": np.array([12, 3, -9]), "Modular Hub": np.array([9, 5, 1])}
emv = {name: float(p @ v) for name, v in payoff.items()}
for name, value in emv.items():
    print(f"EMV({name}) = {value:.2f}")
best = max(emv, key=emv.get)
print(f"Rollback: choose {best}; premium = {max(emv.values()) - min(emv.values()):.2f}")

# ---- Part C: 1,000 reference trials ----
u = pd.read_csv("reference_trials.csv")["u_001"].to_numpy()
mu, sigma, Q, price, salvage, cost = 1000, 250, 1000, 100, 15, 40
profit = lambda d: np.minimum(d, Q) * price + np.maximum(Q - d, 0) * salvage - Q * cost
demand = np.array([NormalDist(mu, sigma).inv_cdf(x) for x in u])   # same as Excel NORM.INV(u, mean, sd)
trials = profit(demand)
print(f"Profit at mean demand  = ${profit(mu):,.0f}")
print(f"Mean simulated profit  = ${trials.mean():,.0f}")
print(f"Sample SD              = ${trials.std(ddof=1):,.0f}")
print(f"5th-percentile profit  = ${np.percentile(trials, 5):,.0f}")   # linear = PERCENTILE.INC
print(f"Flaw-of-averages gap   = ${profit(mu) - trials.mean():,.0f}")
print(f"Trials                 = {trials.size:,}")
R Parts A, B, C

The same checks in base R. quantile(type = 7) matches Excel's PERCENTILE.INC, and qnorm matches NORM.INV.

# LAB02 Parts A-C in R (optional, not graded). Base R only.
# Put this file next to cloudflow_churn_cohort.csv and reference_trials.csv.

# ---- Part A: two-way table and conditional churn risk ----
df <- read.csv("cloudflow_churn_cohort.csv", colClasses = "character", na.strings = "")
pairs <- df[!is.na(df$Churn) & !is.na(df$HighTickets), ]   # complete pairs only
print(addmargins(table(HighTickets = pairs$HighTickets, Churn = pairs$Churn)))
churn <- pairs$Churn == "Yes"
high  <- pairs$HighTickets == "Yes"
pct <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * x)
cat("P(C)       =", pct(mean(churn)), "\n")
cat("P(H)       =", pct(mean(high)), "\n")
cat("P(C and H) =", pct(mean(churn & high)), "\n")
cat("P(C or H)  =", pct(mean(churn) + mean(high) - mean(churn & high)), "\n")
cat("P(H | C)   =", pct(sum(churn & high) / sum(churn)), " <- among churners\n")
cat("P(C | H)   =", pct(sum(churn & high) / sum(high)), " <- among high-ticket accounts\n")

# ---- Part B: payoff table and EMV ($ millions) ----
p   <- c(high = 0.30, medium = 0.50, low = 0.20)
emv <- c(Large = sum(p * c(12, 3, -9)), Modular = sum(p * c(9, 5, 1)))
print(round(emv, 2))
cat("Rollback: choose", names(which.max(emv)), "; premium =", round(max(emv) - min(emv), 2), "\n")

# ---- Part C: 1,000 reference trials ----
u <- read.csv("reference_trials.csv")$u_001
Q <- 1000; price <- 100; salvage <- 15; cost <- 40
profit <- function(d) pmin(d, Q) * price + pmax(Q - d, 0) * salvage - Q * cost
trials <- profit(qnorm(u, mean = 1000, sd = 250))          # same as Excel NORM.INV(u, mean, sd)
dollars <- function(x) paste0("$", format(round(unname(x)), big.mark = ","))
cat("Profit at mean demand =", dollars(profit(1000)), "\n")
cat("Mean simulated profit =", dollars(mean(trials)), "\n")
cat("Sample SD             =", dollars(sd(trials)), "\n")
cat("5th-percentile profit =", dollars(quantile(trials, 0.05, type = 7)), "\n")   # type 7 = PERCENTILE.INC
cat("Flaw-of-averages gap  =", dollars(profit(1000) - mean(trials)), "\n")
cat("Trials                =", length(trials), "\n")

Add a 95% interval next to B18 in a copy of your workbook. In an empty cell type =SQRT(B18*(1-B18)/D9) (the standard error), then =B18-1.96*<that cell> and =B18+1.96*<that cell>. You should get about 29.6% to 41.0%. Is the whole interval above the 12.0% baseline?

SPSS Parts A

The same formula interval in SPSS syntax, built from the two counts in your H1 table.

New code: paste it at the end of LAB02_SPSS.sps, make sure the setup has run this session, then select only the pasted lines and choose Run › Selection.

* How precise is 35.3%? A 95% interval from the counts in your H1 table.
* Type the two counts, then compute the rate, its standard error and the interval.
DATA LIST FREE / churned high_ticket.
BEGIN DATA
96 272
END DATA.
* Rate = churned high-ticket accounts / all high-ticket accounts.
COMPUTE p = churned / high_ticket.
* Standard error of a proportion: square root of p(1 - p) / n.
COMPUTE se = SQRT(p * (1 - p) / high_ticket).
* 95% interval: p plus or minus 1.96 standard errors.
COMPUTE lower = p - 1.96 * se.
COMPUTE upper = p + 1.96 * se.
FORMATS p se lower upper (F6.3).
LIST p se lower upper.
Python Parts A

A bootstrap interval instead of a formula: resample the 272 high-ticket accounts 5,000 times and see how much the rate moves. Compare it with the Excel interval.

# Extension: how precise is the 35.3%? A bootstrap confidence interval for P(Churn | HighTickets).
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("cloudflow_churn_cohort.csv", dtype=str, keep_default_na=False, na_values=[""])
high = df.dropna(subset=["Churn", "HighTickets"]).query("HighTickets == 'Yes'")
churned = high["Churn"].eq("Yes").to_numpy()

rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)                       # fixed seed: same answer every run
boot = [rng.choice(churned, size=churned.size, replace=True).mean() for _ in range(5000)]
low, high_ci = np.percentile(boot, [2.5, 97.5])
print(f"P(C | H) = {churned.mean():.1%}  (n = {churned.size} high-ticket accounts)")
print(f"95% bootstrap interval: {low:.1%} to {high_ci:.1%}")
print("Question: is the interval still well above the 12.0% baseline?")
R Parts A

The same bootstrap in base R with sample() and replicate().

# How precise is 35.3%? Bootstrap the 272 high-ticket accounts 5,000 times.
df <- read.csv("cloudflow_churn_cohort.csv", colClasses = "character", na.strings = "")
high <- df[!is.na(df$Churn) & !is.na(df$HighTickets) & df$HighTickets == "Yes", ]
churned <- high$Churn == "Yes"
set.seed(2026)                                     # fixed seed: same answer every run
boot <- replicate(5000, mean(sample(churned, replace = TRUE)))
ci <- quantile(boot, c(0.025, 0.975))
cat(sprintf("P(C | H) = %.1f%% (n = %d)\n", 100 * mean(churned), length(churned)))
cat(sprintf("95%% bootstrap interval: %.1f%% to %.1f%%\n", 100 * ci[1], 100 * ci[2]))

Add expected counts, the chi-square test and phi to the H1 crosstab. Compare the Yes/Yes observed and expected counts.

DATASET ACTIVATE CohortData.

Python Parts A

The chi-square test computed by hand, so you can see every step: observed, expected, the statistic and the p-value.

# Is the churn / high-ticket pattern more than chance? A chi-square test by hand.
import math
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("cloudflow_churn_cohort.csv", dtype=str, keep_default_na=False, na_values=[""])
pairs = df.dropna(subset=["Churn", "HighTickets"])
observed = pd.crosstab(pairs["HighTickets"], pairs["Churn"])
n = observed.to_numpy().sum()
# Expected count if the two were unrelated: row total x column total / n
expected = pd.DataFrame(
    [[observed.loc[r].sum() * observed[c].sum() / n for c in observed.columns] for r in observed.index],
    index=observed.index, columns=observed.columns)
chi_sq = (((observed - expected) ** 2) / expected).to_numpy().sum()
p_value = math.erfc(math.sqrt(chi_sq / 2))          # exact for a 2 x 2 table (1 degree of freedom)
phi = math.sqrt(chi_sq / n)
print("Observed:\n", observed, "\n\nExpected if unrelated:\n", expected.round(1))
print(f"\nChi-square = {chi_sq:.1f}, p-value = {p_value:.2g}, phi = {phi:.2f}")
print("A small p-value says the pattern is unlikely to be chance. It still does not show that screening prevents churn.")
R Parts A

One line in R: chisq.test(). A small p-value still says nothing about cause.

# Extension: is the churn / high-ticket association more than chance?
df <- read.csv("cloudflow_churn_cohort.csv", colClasses = "character", na.strings = "")
pairs <- df[!is.na(df$Churn) & !is.na(df$HighTickets), ]
tab <- table(HighTickets = pairs$HighTickets, Churn = pairs$Churn)
test <- chisq.test(tab)
print(tab)
print(round(test$expected, 1))                               # counts expected if there were no association
print(test)
# A small p-value says the pattern is unlikely to be chance.
# It still does not show that screening would prevent churn.

Python Parts C

Sweep capacities from 700 to 1,500 on the same 1,000 trials, then compare the best one with the newsvendor critical-ratio formula Q∗=F−1 ⁣(p−cp−s) Q^* = F^{-1}\!\left(\frac{p-c}{p-s}\right) .

# Extension: which capacity maximizes expected profit? (the newsvendor problem)
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from statistics import NormalDist

u = pd.read_csv("reference_trials.csv")["u_001"].to_numpy()
demand = np.array([NormalDist(1000, 250).inv_cdf(x) for x in u])
price, salvage, cost = 100, 15, 40

def mean_profit(Q):
    return (np.minimum(demand, Q) * price + np.maximum(Q - demand, 0) * salvage - Q * cost).mean()

capacities = np.arange(700, 1501, 25)
results = pd.DataFrame({"capacity": capacities, "mean_profit": [mean_profit(q) for q in capacities]})
best = results.loc[results["mean_profit"].idxmax()]
print(results.to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda x: f"{x:,.0f}"))
print(f"\nBest simulated capacity: {best.capacity:.0f} units, mean profit ${best.mean_profit:,.0f}")

# Theory check: the critical ratio says order up to the (p - c) / (p - s) quantile of demand.
ratio = (price - cost) / (price - salvage)
print(f"Critical ratio = {ratio:.3f} -> Q* = {NormalDist(1000, 250).inv_cdf(ratio):,.0f} units")
R Parts C

The same sweep in base R, with a plot of mean profit against capacity.

# Which capacity maximizes expected profit? Same 1,000 trials, capacities 700 to 1,500.
u <- read.csv("reference_trials.csv")$u_001
demand <- qnorm(u, mean = 1000, sd = 250)
price <- 100; salvage <- 15; cost <- 40
mean_profit <- function(Q) mean(pmin(demand, Q) * price + pmax(Q - demand, 0) * salvage - Q * cost)
caps <- seq(700, 1500, by = 25)
profits <- sapply(caps, mean_profit)
plot(caps, profits, type = "b", xlab = "Capacity (units)", ylab = "Mean profit ($)", main = "Expected profit by capacity")
best <- caps[which.max(profits)]
cat("Best simulated capacity:", best, "units, mean profit $", format(round(max(profits)), big.mark = ","), "\n")
ratio <- (price - cost) / (price - salvage)
cat("Critical ratio", round(ratio, 3), "-> Q* =", round(qnorm(ratio, 1000, 250)), "units\n")

Excel Parts B

In a copy, set D7 to =1-B7-C7 so the probabilities always total 100%, and put =D14-D15 in an empty cell such as F14. Choose Data › What-If Analysis › Goal Seek: set F14 to 0 by changing B7. The answer is the P(high demand) at which both hubs tie.

SPSS Parts B

A small grid of P(high) values with both EMVs side by side. Find the first row where large_wins turns to 1.

New code: paste it at the end of LAB02_SPSS.sps, make sure the setup has run this session, then select only the pasted lines and choose Run › Selection.

* Where does the hub decision flip? Keep P(medium) = 0.50 and try P(high) from 0 to 0.50.
DATA LIST FREE / p_high.
BEGIN DATA
0 .05 .10 .15 .20 .25 .30 .35 .40 .45 .50
END DATA.
* P(low) is whatever is left so the three probabilities total 1.
COMPUTE p_low = 0.50 - p_high.
* EMV = sum of probability x payoff ($ millions) for each hub.
COMPUTE emv_large = p_high * 12 + 0.50 * 3 + p_low * (-9).
COMPUTE emv_modular = p_high * 9 + 0.50 * 5 + p_low * 1.
COMPUTE large_wins = (emv_large > emv_modular).
FORMATS p_high p_low (F4.2) emv_large emv_modular (F6.2) large_wins (F1.0).
LIST.
Python Parts B

The same grid in Python, plus the exact tipping point from setting the two EMV lines equal.

# Where does the hub decision flip? Keep P(medium) = 0.50 and vary P(high demand).
import numpy as np

large, modular = np.array([12, 3, -9]), np.array([9, 5, 1])      # payoffs in $ millions: high, medium, low
p_high = np.round(np.arange(0, 0.51, 0.05), 2)
rows = []
for ph in p_high:
    probs = np.array([ph, 0.50, 0.50 - ph])
    rows.append((ph, probs @ large, probs @ modular))
print("P(high)  EMV Large  EMV Modular")
for ph, el, em in rows:
    print(f"{ph:7.2f} {el:10.2f} {em:12.2f}" + ("   <- Large wins" if el > em else ""))
# Exact: EMV(Large) = 21p - 3 and EMV(Modular) = 8p + 3, so they tie at p = 6/13
print(f"\nTipping point: P(high) = {6/13:.3f}. Today's forecast is 0.30.")
R Parts B

Plot both EMVs as P(high demand) changes and find the tipping point exactly with uniroot. How far is today's 30% forecast from it?

# Extension: when would the Large Hub win? Keep P(medium) = 0.50 and vary P(high demand).
ph <- seq(0, 0.50, by = 0.01)
emv_large   <- 12 * ph + 3 * 0.50 + (-9) * (0.50 - ph)
emv_modular <-  9 * ph + 5 * 0.50 +    1 * (0.50 - ph)
plot(ph, emv_large, type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "firebrick",
     ylim = range(c(emv_large, emv_modular)),
     xlab = "P(high demand)", ylab = "EMV ($ millions)", main = "Where the decision flips")
lines(ph, emv_modular, lwd = 2, col = "purple")
abline(v = 0.30, lty = 2)                                   # today's forecast
legend("topleft", c("Large Hub", "Modular Hub"), col = c("firebrick", "purple"), lwd = 2)
tip <- uniroot(function(x) (21 * x - 3) - (8 * x + 3), c(0, 0.5))$root
cat("The Large Hub overtakes the Modular Hub when P(high) exceeds", round(tip, 3), "\n")
